summary:
Colima is a state of Mexico, and its trans-visitor exposure is set by Mexico's national framework rather than by any local statute identified in the sources reviewed. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised anywhere in the country, and same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction. Nothing in the inventory indicates that Colima has enacted a law targeting trans presence.

Legal gender recognition remains a state-by-state question. The Human Rights Watch report of 31 March 2025 counted, as of March 2025, 22 of Mexico's 32 states that had legislated an administrative procedure, two further states that operate a procedure in practice without having enacted one, six legislatures that have enacted nothing at all, and only seven states that extend recognition to minors. The Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation set binding guidelines for the states in 2022 and extended the right to minors, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. HRW has called on the states that still lack such procedures to adopt them, and warned that implementation differs sharply from one state to another.

Whether Colima has enacted an administrative recognition procedure, and whether it extends recognition to children, is not established in the material reviewed here. The operative point for a visitor is the national picture: where a state procedure is absent, HRW documents that identity-document mismatch drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco.

What an absent procedure means on the ground is set out in the joint HRW and Community Center for Inclusion report of 6 March 2024, produced from Tabasco, one of the states with no legal gender-recognition procedure. Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, the report finds that every document request and every appearance-based scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and that trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. The account is Tabasco's, and the sources reviewed do not carry a parallel study of Colima, but the same procedural vacuum is what a trans visitor without matching documents should expect to encounter wherever Colima's own procedure is missing.

The enforcement backdrop is severe. More than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished in 2022, and impunity for transfemicide is thought to be higher still. Transgender Europe's monitoring counts 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100 in the same period. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. In January 2024, AP reported at least three transgender people killed in the opening weeks of the year, among them the activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests.

Transfemicide has begun to be treated as a distinct crime, but only in some states. Nayarit criminalised it first, with penalties up to 60 years, and Mexico City's Congress passed the 'Paola Buenrostro law' in July 2024, punishable by up to 70 years; the statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. Colima's legislature has not been shown in the sources reviewed to have enacted a comparable offence.

The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP of 22 November 2024 concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice; the analysis explicitly cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.
tangentialFactors:
Colima is one of 32 Mexican states, and the pattern its visitors stand under is national: a majority of states now run some form of administrative legal gender recognition, but a substantial minority do not, and the seven states that recognise minors are the exception rather than the rule. Two states operate a procedure in practice without enacting it, which means recognition can depend on the disposition of an office rather than on written law.

Tabasco is the clearest named data point for the risk created by an absent procedure, documented in detail in the HRW and Community Center for Inclusion report of 6 March 2024; the same report records the August 2023 murder of the trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa. Guanajuato supplies the second named example, with incidents of discrimination linked to document mismatch recorded there. Neither state is Colima, and the sources reviewed contain no reporting specific to Colima's own recognition practice.

The transfemicide-crime trend is also concentrated outside Colima on the available evidence: Nayarit and Mexico City are the two states named as having criminalised transfemicide, with penalties of up to 60 and 70 years respectively. The national homicide-impunity figure of more than 95% in 2022 and the higher estimated transfemicide impunity apply throughout, including to states without a dedicated offence.
localsOnly:
Residents of Colima are subject to the Supreme Court's binding recognition guidelines set in 2022, which include the extension of legal gender recognition to minors, and to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requirement that the procedure be simple and accessible. These standards bind the state legislature even where no local procedure has been enacted, and HRW's 31 March 2025 appeal is directed precisely at the states that have yet to legislate.

Marriage equality is settled for residents as well: same-sex marriage has been legal in Mexico since 2009, and partnership recognition is not a point of dispute at the national level.

The practical finding for residents is that formal rights have not translated into uniform access. Beer's 22 November 2024 analysis reports that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, and HRW's March 2025 account documents the consequences where recognition is absent or obstructed, including discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market.

Residents face the same impunity environment as visitors: more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022, and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights warned in 2024 that impunity for LGBTI+ violations may have reached alarming levels, while insisting that such violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Colima has enacted an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition is unresolved in the sources reviewed. HRW's 31 March 2025 count gives national totals only: 22 states with enacted procedures, two operating one without legislation, six with nothing enacted. Colima's individual position within that count is not stated and has not been verified here.

Whether Colima's legislature criminalises transfemicide is likewise not sourced. The inventory names Nayarit and Mexico City as the two states that have done so; no Colima statute is cited, and this should not be read as a finding that Colima has none, only as an absence of evidence in the material reviewed.

Local homicide, transfemicide and impunity figures for Colima specifically are not available in the sources reviewed. The 95%-plus national impunity figure for 2022 and the Transgender Europe monitoring counts are national aggregates and are not broken down to Colima.

No Colima-specific reporting on trans violence, on document-related discrimination, or on the operation of any local recognition procedure was included in the source inventory. The Tabasco findings are attributed to Tabasco, and the Guanajuato incidents to Guanajuato; neither should be quoted as documented experience within Colima.

The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights recommendations of 2024 are addressed to federal and state authorities generally and are not addressed to Colima by name.
